title: Preferred Stimulation Levels in Introverts and Extraverts: Effects on Arousal and Performance

findings.antecedent: Personality type (extravert vs. introvert)
findings.mechanism: Extraverts seek higher levels of stimulation due to lower cortical arousal, introverts seek lower levels due to higher cortical arousal.
findings.quote: The mean setting for introverts was 37.3, and for extraverts it was 54.2, t(18) = 2.72, p < .01.

findings.antecedent: Treatment condition or personality type
findings.mechanism: Ensuring no pre-existing physiological differences before experimental manipulation.
findings.quote: No differences were found in PR across either the treatment or personality variables among data from the baseline measure.

findings.antecedent: Choice vs. Assigned-same condition (for same personality type)
findings.mechanism: The mere act of choosing stimulation level does not inherently alter physiological arousal compared to receiving the same chosen level.
findings.quote: PR in each of the assigned-same conditions did not differ from that in the appropriate choice condition.

findings.antecedent: Personality type (introvert vs. extravert) when stimulated at their own preferred noise level (or yoked-same-type)
findings.mechanism: Individuals adjust stimulation to achieve their optimal level of arousal, leading to comparable arousal states across personality types.
findings.quote: As long as introverts and extraverts received noise at a level equal to that chosen by members of the same respective type, they showed equal rates.

findings.antecedent: Personality type (introvert vs. extravert) in assigned conditions
findings.mechanism: Introverts are more excitable or arousable than extraverts in response to given levels of stimulation.
findings.quote: main effects for both E-I, F(1, 36) = 8.67, p < .01... At both levels of intensity, introverts showed higher pulse rates than extraverts.

findings.antecedent: Noise intensity level (introvert-chosen vs. extravert-chosen) in assigned conditions
findings.mechanism: Higher stimulation levels generally lead to increased physiological arousal.

findings.mechanism: No significant changes in peripheral vasoconstriction were observed.
findings.quote: The measure of finger pulse volume did not show any significant effects during either baseline or treatment periods.

findings.antecedent: Treatment condition or personality type
findings.mechanism: Ensuring no pre-existing physiological differences before experimental manipulation.
findings.quote: baseline period showed no significant differences among conditions.

findings.antecedent: Choice vs. Assigned-same condition (for same personality type)
findings.mechanism: The mere act of choosing stimulation level does not inherently alter physiological arousal compared to receiving the same chosen level.
findings.quote: The assigned-same condition did not differ from the choice condition.

findings.antecedent: Personality type (introvert vs. extravert) when stimulated at their own preferred noise level (or yoked-same-type)
findings.mechanism: Individuals adjust stimulation to achieve their optimal level of arousal, leading to comparable arousal states across personality types.
findings.quote: Introverts and extraverts receiving stimulation at a level chosen by members of similar personality type showed equal numbers of SRRs.

findings.antecedent: Personality type (introvert vs. extravert) in assigned conditions
findings.mechanism: Introverts are more excitable or arousable than extraverts in response to given levels of stimulation.
findings.quote: main effects for E-I, F(1, 36) = 7.46, p < .01... introverts show evidence of greater arousal than extraverts.

findings.antecedent: Noise intensity level (introvert-chosen vs. extravert-chosen) in assigned conditions
findings.mechanism: Higher stimulation levels generally lead to increased physiological arousal.
findings.quote: and noise intensity, F(1, 36) = 6.32, p < .05.

findings.antecedent: Choice vs. Assigned-same condition (for same personality type)
findings.mechanism: The act of choosing stimulation does not inherently affect task performance when the chosen level is maintained.
findings.quote: the mere fact of choice did not influence performance

findings.antecedent: Personality type (introvert vs. extravert) when stimulated at their own preferred noise level (or yoked-same-type)
findings.mechanism: Optimal arousal levels, achieved through preferred stimulation, lead to comparable task performance across personality types, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson Law.
findings.quote: Under these conditions introverts and extraverts performed equally well.

findings.antecedent: Interaction of Personality type (E-I) and Noise intensity level (introvert-chosen vs. extravert-chosen)
findings.mechanism: The effect of noise intensity on performance is dependent on personality type, reflecting different optimal arousal levels.
findings.quote: significant interaction between E-I and noise intensity level, F(1, 36) = 10.64, p < .01.

findings.antecedent: Introverts stimulated at noise level preferred by extraverts
findings.mechanism: Noise levels preferred by extraverts lead to overstimulation for introverts, impairing their performance according to the Yerkes-Dodson Law.
findings.quote: Introverts performed significantly less well than extraverts when stimulated at a level preferred by extraverts

findings.antecedent: Extraverts stimulated at noise level preferred by introverts
findings.mechanism: Noise levels preferred by introverts lead to suboptimal stimulation for extraverts, but not necessarily to a significant impairment in performance compared to introverts at that level.
findings.quote: extraverts did not differ from introverts when stimulated at a level preferred by introverts.

findings.antecedent: Personality type (extravert vs. introvert)
findings.mechanism: Extraverts seek higher levels of stimulation due to lower cortical arousal, introverts seek lower levels due to higher cortical arousal.
findings.quote: The mean noise intensity setting chosen was 50.4 and that of introverts 31.1. The difference between the two means was significant, t(18) = 3.60, p < .01.

findings.antecedent: Introverts' chosen noise intensity (lowest acceptable vs. optimal)
findings.mechanism: Individuals can identify a range of acceptable stimulation levels around their optimal point.
findings.quote: The lowest acceptable intensity setting chosen by introverts was 21.1, which was significantly lower than 31.1, t(9) = 3.34, p < .01.

findings.antecedent: Extraverts' chosen noise intensity (highest acceptable vs. optimal)
findings.mechanism: Individuals can identify a range of acceptable stimulation levels around their optimal point.
findings.quote: highest acceptable setting chosen by extraverts was 57.5, which was significantly higher than 50.4, t(9) = 4.53, p < .01.

findings.antecedent: Treatment condition or personality type
findings.mechanism: Ensuring no pre-existing physiological differences before experimental manipulation.
findings.quote: No differences for baseline measures were found.

findings.antecedent: Personality type (introvert vs. extravert)
findings.mechanism: Introverts are generally more aroused than extraverts across varying stimulation levels.
findings.quote: significant effects for E-I, F(1, 72) = 15.50, p < .01

findings.antecedent: Noise intensity level (Low, Mod-low, Mod-high, High)
findings.mechanism: Physiological arousal increases with increasing stimulus intensity.
findings.quote: the level of noise intensity, F(3, 72) = 17.98, p < .01

findings.antecedent: Interaction of Personality type (E-I) and Noise intensity level
findings.mechanism: The relationship between stimulation and arousal is curvilinear and differs between introverts and extraverts, with introverts peaking at lower stimulation levels.
findings.quote: the interaction between the two, F(3, 72) = 2.76, p < .05.

findings.antecedent: Personality type (introvert vs. extravert) at Low or High noise intensity
findings.mechanism: At very low or very high stimulation levels, central inhibitory processes (transmarginal inhibition) may equalize arousal across personality types.
findings.quote: introverts were equal to extraverts in PR in response to both the most intense and least intense level of noise

findings.antecedent: Personality type (introvert vs. extravert) at Mod-low or Mod-high noise intensity
findings.mechanism: Introverts are more aroused than extraverts at moderate stimulation levels, consistent with Eysenck's theory.
findings.quote: introverts showed higher PR in response to both of the intermediate levels of noise.

findings.antecedent: Noise intensity level (Low, Mod-low, Mod-high, High)
findings.mechanism: Performance follows an inverted U-shaped curve with respect to arousal, as described by the Yerkes-Dodson Law.
findings.quote: significant effects for noise intensity, F(3, 72) = 4.68, p < .01

findings.antecedent: Interaction of Personality type (E-I) and Noise intensity level
findings.mechanism: The optimal arousal level for performance, and thus the optimal stimulation level, differs between introverts and extraverts.
findings.quote: the interaction of noise intensity with E-I, F(3, 72) = 8.29; p < .01.

findings.antecedent: Introverts stimulated at Mod-low noise intensity (their optimal)
findings.mechanism: Optimal stimulation leads to optimal arousal, resulting in the best performance for introverts.
findings.quote: Both introverts and extraverts required fewer trials to reach criterion when stimulated at an intensity level chosen by each of them.

findings.antecedent: Extraverts stimulated at Mod-high noise intensity (their optimal)
findings.mechanism: Optimal stimulation leads to optimal arousal, resulting in the best performance for extraverts.
findings.quote: Both introverts and extraverts required fewer trials to reach criterion when stimulated at an intensity level chosen by each of them.

findings.antecedent: Introverts stimulated at Mod-high or High noise intensity
findings.mechanism: Overstimulation for introverts leads to arousal levels beyond optimal, impairing performance according to the Yerkes-Dodson Law.
findings.quote: Introverts showed poorer performance when stimulated by noise at the two higher levels of intensity

findings.antecedent: Introverts stimulated at Low noise intensity (below their optimal)
findings.mechanism: Suboptimal stimulation for introverts leads to arousal levels below optimal, impairing performance according to the Yerkes-Dodson Law.
findings.quote: no significant decrement when stimulated at a level below their optimal level.

findings.antecedent: Extraverts stimulated at Low noise intensity (below their optimal)
findings.mechanism: Suboptimal stimulation for extraverts leads to arousal levels below optimal, impairing performance according to the Yerkes-Dodson Law.
findings.quote: Extraverts, however, showed a decrement in performance with deviations from the optimal level in both an upward and downward direction.

findings.antecedent: Extraverts stimulated at High noise intensity (above their optimal)
findings.mechanism: Overstimulation for extraverts leads to arousal levels beyond optimal, impairing performance according to the Yerkes-Dodson Law.
findings.quote: Extraverts, however, showed a decrement in performance with deviations from the optimal level in both an upward and downward direction.

stimuli.description: Recorded white noise delivered in random short bursts (1s duration, 10s interval) at varying intensity levels (0-100 dial units, estimated 40-85 dB SPL).

tables.description: Mean Trials to Criterion (Experiment 1) for Extraverts and Introverts across different noise treatments (Choice, Assigned introvert choice, Assigned extravert choice).
Mean Trials to Criterion (Experiment 2) for Extraverts and Introverts across four noise conditions (Low, Mod-low, Mod-high, High).

limitations: Conductance data were collected for only slightly more than half the subjects in Experiment 2 due to apparatus malfunction.
The estimates of the four intensity levels in decibels were approximations only.
The study focused on the relation between arousal and the E-I variable per se, acknowledging that other investigators suggest impulsivity might be the critical linking variable.
The Yerkes-Dodson Law is an empirical generalization and does not explain the underlying causes of the arousal-performance relationship.
